rationale: A wins because it knows what it can prove and makes the missing proof part of the strategy, not wallpaper. Its strongest headline, "Companies are paying an average of $342,000 a year for software nobody is using, Ramp beta data shows," stays inside the facts and immediately names the reporting test. B has useful bones, but lines like "As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" turn a decent contrarian angle into a fact-shaped guess wearing a press badge.
gaps_in_A: "AI agents are moving into real finance work" is the weakest headline in A: true enough, but broad enough to attract generic AI-trend coverage unless the approval-flow and rejection-rate proof exists.

"software vendors' renewal playbooks ... now face an automated auditor" slightly outruns the supplied evidence; the update proves drafted emails and flagged waste, not vendor behavior or actual renewal pressure.
"compete on money saved rather than money processed" is a smart business-strategy hypothesis, but it needs market context the update does not supply.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" overstates the product. The update says the agent drafts emails that finance approves; B turns assisted drafting into vendor contact.
"initiating a real-world business transaction" is agentic-AI puffery unless Ramp can prove what is sent, by whom, and with what authority.
"The average company wastes $342,000 a year" universalizes a 200-company Ramp beta and quietly drops the sample boundary. That is how a usable number becomes a complaint from a fact-checker.
"As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is the big sin: the angle depends on an assumption the update never gives. "Presumably" is not a source.
